texts.profile:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: The Leaf's Sugar Factory

INTRO: This is practice, not a score: a wrong answer only shows what to look at next. You have enough background, so we go straight to the core reaction.

SECTION 1 - The core reaction
Photosynthesis is how plants make glucose (sugar) from carbon dioxide and water. The plant uses light energy, from the sun, to drive that change. Takeaway: the plant builds sugar from two raw materials using light.
EXAMPLE: Try it: What two raw materials does a plant use to make glucose? Answer: carbon dioxide and water.

SECTION 2 - The light absorber and the by-product
Chlorophyll, the green pigment in chloroplasts, absorbs the light. Photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, which hold many chloroplasts. Oxygen is released as a by-product, not used as an input. Takeaway: chlorophyll captures light in leaves, and oxygen leaves as waste.
EXAMPLE: Try it: A comic shows a leaf as a solar panel. Which pigment is the panel's light absorber? Answer: chlorophyll.

SECTION 3 - The chain to remember
Picture the reaction as an arrow chain: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll is the light absorber, not a raw material. Leaves are the main site, so most of the chain happens there. Takeaway: light energy lets chlorophyll in leaf chloroplasts turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen.
EXAMPLE: Try it: In a game, a plant has water and light but no carbon dioxide. What raw material is missing for making glucose? Answer: carbon dioxide.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A basketball player exhales carbon dioxide near a sunlit leaf. Trace the leaf's photosynthesis in order.
  1. Carbon dioxide from the air enters the leaf; reasoning: carbon dioxide is one raw material.
  2. Water arrives from the roots; reasoning: water is the other raw material.
  3. Chlorophyll in the leaf's chloroplasts absorbs light energy from the sun; reasoning: chlorophyll is the pigment that captures light.
  4. The light energy powers the build of glucose from carbon dioxide and water; reasoning: glucose is the sugar product.
  5. Oxygen exits the leaf as a by-product; reasoning: oxygen is released, not kept as the main product.
  ANSWER: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen, mainly in the leaf.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: Plants use light energy to turn oxygen and glucose into carbon dioxide and water. Why: this reverses the reaction; oxygen is a by-product and glucose is made, not a raw material. Right: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis mostly happens in leaves: chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs sunlight, and light energy turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Which product is the sugar that a plant makes and keeps during photosynthesis? [choices: Glucose | Oxygen | Chlorophyll | Carbon dioxide] -> Glucose
2. A leaf has water and light but no carbon dioxide. What raw material is missing for making glucose? [typed answer] -> carbon dioxide
texts.mirror:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: How a Plant Makes Its Own Food

INTRO: A plant cannot walk to a shop, so it builds its own food inside its leaves. That building job is called photosynthesis. This lesson walks you through the recipe, the power source, and what comes out at the end.

SECTION 1 - The recipe: two ingredients and one product
Photosynthesis is how a plant makes its own food. The plant builds a sugar called glucose from two ingredients: carbon dioxide and water. Carbon dioxide is a gas in the air, and water is drawn up from the soil through the roots. Light energy from the sun powers the joining, but light is not an ingredient itself. So the recipe is: carbon dioxide + water, powered by light, gives glucose.
EXAMPLE: Picture a game level where you place two plants in a room that has air and water. Plant A sits by a bright window. Plant B sits in a dark cupboard with the door shut. Step 1: check the ingredients. Both plants have carbon dioxide from the air and water, so the ingredients are not the problem. Step 2: check the energy. Plant A gets light energy; Plant B gets none. Last step for you: which plant makes glucose, and what is missing for the other? Answer: Plant A makes glucose, because light energy powers the joining of carbon dioxide and water. Plant B has no light energy, so that joining cannot happen.

SECTION 2 - Chlorophyll: the light catcher
The plant needs something to catch the light, and that job belongs to chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the green colouring inside a leaf, and it absorbs the light energy, which means it soaks it up. Chlorophyll sits inside chloroplasts, which are tiny green parts inside plant cells. The energy that chlorophyll soaks up is what drives the joining of carbon dioxide and water. Only green parts have chlorophyll, so only green parts can catch light for this job.
EXAMPLE: Here is the same recipe as a labelled chain you can read left to right. carbon dioxide (from the air) + water (from the soil) -- light energy (absorbed by chlorophyll inside chloroplasts) --> glucose (the plant's sugar) + oxygen (released as a by-product). The two things on the left are the ingredients. The label on the arrow is the power source. The two things on the right are what the plant ends up with.

SECTION 3 - Oxygen out, and mostly in the leaves
Oxygen is made at the same time as the glucose, and it leaves the plant through tiny holes in the leaf surface. Oxygen is a by-product here, which means something made along the way that is not the main product the plant was after. Photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, because leaves are flat and wide, which gives them a lot of surface to catch light. Leaves also hold most of the plant's chloroplasts, and water arrives there from the roots.
EXAMPLE: Try it: a water plant in a bright tank has tiny bubbles forming on its leaves. Which gas is inside the bubbles, and why does the plant release it? Answer: oxygen, because oxygen is the by-product released when the plant makes glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

WORKED EXAMPLE: You are drawing a comic panel of a plant on a windowsill, and a reader asks what the plant is actually doing. Trace the whole job in five steps.
  1. Name the ingredients. Carbon dioxide drifts in from the air, and water comes up from the soil through the roots. These two are the starting materials.
  2. Name the power source. Sunlight lands on the leaf and powers the job. Light is energy here, not a material, so it does not become part of the sugar.
  3. Name the light catcher. Inside leaf cells are chloroplasts, tiny green parts. They hold chlorophyll, the green colouring that absorbs the light energy.
  4. Name the product. The light energy lets the plant join carbon dioxide and water into glucose, a sugar. That glucose is the plant's food.
  5. Name what is left over. Oxygen is made along the way and leaves the leaf as a by-product.
  ANSWER: carbon dioxide + water, powered by light energy absorbed by chlorophyll inside chloroplasts, gives glucose + oxygen. Most of this happens in the leaves.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: plants take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide to make glucose. Why: the two gases are swapped; the plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen, and that oxygen is a by-product of making glucose. Right: carbon dioxide + water, powered by light energy, gives glucose + oxygen.
Wrong: sunlight is an ingredient in the glucose, so the plant's sugar is partly made of light. Why: light is energy, not a material, so it powers the joining of carbon dioxide and water but does not become part of the glucose. Right: the glucose is built from carbon dioxide and water only, with light energy driving the joining.
Wrong: photosynthesis happens in the roots, because that is where the water is. Why: the water travels up to the leaves, and the light is caught there, so the roots are not the main site. Right: photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, where chlorophyll inside chloroplasts absorbs the light energy.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis is how a plant builds glucose, a sugar, from carbon dioxide and water. Light energy from the sun powers that joining, and chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts of leaf cells absorbs the light. Oxygen is released along the way as a by-product, and the whole job happens mainly in the leaves.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Hint: think of the two starting materials. Which gas does a plant take in from the air to make glucose? [choices: Oxygen | Carbon dioxide | Nitrogen | Water vapour] -> Carbon dioxide
2. Hint: the ingredients are all there, so look at the power source. A leaf is kept in a dark cupboard with air and water for a day. Explain why it cannot make glucose. [typed answer] -> There is no light, so there is no light energy to power the joining of carbon dioxide and water into glucose.
3. Hint: check each sentence against the recipe, the light catcher, the by-product and the main site. Which sentence is completely correct? [choices: Plants use sunlight as an ingredient that becomes part of the glucose. | Chlorophyll inside chloroplasts absorbs light energy, and oxygen leaves the plant as a by-product. | Photosynthesis happens mainly in the roots, because that is where the water enters. | Plants turn oxygen and water into sugar, and release carbon dioxide.] -> Chlorophyll inside chloroplasts absorbs light energy, and oxygen leaves the plant as a by-product.
